text: Track 1.1 Good morning, Sally. Thank you for joining us today. My first question might be an obvious one. What are GM foods? Well, as some of you may know, GM foods are plants, like corn, rice, bananas, and many more, which have been changed by scientists in a way that does not occur in nature. For example, in simple terms, if a scientist wants to make red bananas, they can get a red plant, cut out a piece of it that carries the information for red color, and insert it into the banana. They then plant the new banana seed, and the tree will produce red bananas instead of yellow. Wow, that sounds amazing. But are these foods good for us? Well, that's a difficult question to answer. GM foods have been changed by scientists, but despite what some people claim, there's no evidence that they are actually bad for us to eat. So I wouldn't avoid them. People have been trying to find a way to end world hunger for many years, and GM foods may be part of the solution. They could feed millions of people around the world, and that's the reason for my interest, not particularly because I want to see red bananas. Of course, can you tell us more about why scientists make these changes to plants? Well, sometimes for health reasons. For instance, changes like these can be used to increase the amount of vitamins in a food. In one project, food scientists made changes to rice so that it contained more vitamin A, and was healthier than ordinary rice. This healthy rice was then sent to countries where people had poor diets, and were getting sick. Is that the only reason food is changed? No, there are a number of reasons. For example, scientists can make certain vegetables like tomatoes grow bigger. Also, in areas where agriculture can be challenging, farmers can use these changed plants to grow foods in bad conditions that are not typically suitable for growing crops. This is extremely helpful in countries that are very dry or have little rain. That's interesting. It is, and these days, this type of produce is becoming even more critical, as farming conditions are expected to get worse in many areas due to the effects of rising temperatures and climate change. And of all the issues facing agricultural industries, climate change is, in my personal opinion, the number one challenge. Absolutely. Are these crops more expensive to produce? Well, that's an interesting question. Generally, production costs are lower because farmers do not need to use expensive chemicals. This is because scientists can improve the quality of the crop so that it fights diseases, which means that these plants can protect themselves from bugs and other pests that normally harm it. Recently, however, some scientists who have investigated the relationship between these foods and disease argue that crops may need more chemicals. Because as the crop gets stronger, the bugs and pests do too. So you see, some scientists support this process, while others remain a bit doubtful about the long-term effects, as these still remain unknown. What about the farmers themselves? Does anything change for them? Well, yes, agricultural crops can become the property of a private company, which means that the company, often a large, multinational one, owns the crop, and therefore decides what can and cannot be done with it. This can have a negative effect on the farmers. How so? OK, so normally farmers keep some seeds from their current crop when it is harvested. They do this so they can plant the seeds the following year. Obviously, this saves money, as the farmer doesn't need to buy the seeds they are going to plant. But if, for example, a company owns the crop and can make all the farming decisions, that company may require farmers to purchase new seeds from them. Of course, this might mean the farmers' costs increase and their profits decrease. I see. It's not straightforward, is it? Right, thank you for joining us today, Sally. I'm afraid that's all we have time for.
